paragraphs.text: God, as the lover of mankind, has always given sinners time for repentance; but the negligent man destroys his own soul through his sloth. For by loving what is vain, earthly and fleeting, he deprives himself of the enjoyment of the heavenly goods. Man, whom his Maker and God appointed king and lord of all, has become a slave of sin through worldly desires. That is why David says of those who do such things: “They have not known, nor have they understood; they walk on in darkness.” And Christ, alluding to sinners, says: “They do not come to the light, so that their deeds may not be exposed; for everyone who does evil hates the light.” And again he says: “While you have the light, walk toward the light, so that darkness may not overtake you.” And again he says: “I came into the world so that they may not perish, but may have life.” And again: “I did not come to judge the world, but to save it.” And again: “I lay down my life for the sheep.” The harlot heard these words, which were proclaimed everywhere like perfumes and gave the fragrance of life to all who were worthy. She called her evil deeds to mind and at once took hold of these words. She wept over the shame of what she had done and thought about the evils that would come upon her because of it, for great affliction and anguish await fornicators there. Out of this fear the harlot was changed. She no longer remained a harlot, but at once became more chaste than a virgin. For she sat down alone, set up a court within herself, and condemned herself, saying: “Woe is me, the sinner! Woe is me, the profligate! How long will I not turn away from evil? Why do I not consider the compassion of God? For the Master goes about every road for my sake, for I have wandered like a sheep. For my sake he bowed the heavens and came down; for my sake he who gives food to all flesh dines with a sinful Pharisee. The sinless one draws near to the sinner; he who feeds everyone shares a table; he who is borne upon the cherubim reclines on the ground and forgives all sinners the bonds of their sins. Why then do you still wait? Take courage, my soul, draw near: he did not come to save the righteous, but sinners.” As soon as she had said this, the fragrance of forgiveness came upon her from Christ's table. Once she had been profligate, but now she was chaste; once a wild beast, but now a sheep; once a slave of sin, but now set free by repentance; once a harlot, but now modest. And resolved with an eager soul to seek his help, she comes to him. When she saw the Master at the table, she did not ask for crumbs, as the Canaanite woman did, but embraced the whole bread of life himself. For the Canaanite woman pleaded for her daughter, who was possessed by a demon, and when she heard herself called a dog, she asked to receive crumbs. This woman did not have a demon-possessed daughter; her own whole body was possessed by licentiousness. The Canaanite woman cried out in front of everyone, “Have mercy on me, Son of David!” The harlot, however, let out no cry. She saw that as God he knows all things, so she kept her mouth silent and spoke with her heart to the one who knows hearts. Weeping, she kissed his feet, and so she moved the Master to compassion. But I wish, brothers, to search the mind of that wise woman and to learn how Christ received her and how he shone upon her darkened soul. For truly, as David prophesied, “The Lord is fairer in beauty than the sons of men”; and he is not only fair, but also a lover of what is fair. For even before she came in to him, he recognized that her soul had a good resolve. But if you please, let us also hear the words of the Gospel: “While Jesus was reclining at table in the house of the Pharisee, a certain woman in the city who was a sinner heard of it. She took precious ointment, came in, and anointed his feet, wet them with her tears, and wiped them with her hair.” Great was the woman's zeal, great her race toward salvation, great the resolve of a soul that wished to be freed from danger! She heard and she hurried. She drove her thoughts toward repentance, saying within herself: “O sinful and thrice-wretched soul, what are you waiting for? What are you pondering? Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Behold, the time you were seeking has come; behold, he is here who loosens, cleanses and scours away sins; the ointment is here. How long will you linger in the mire and the stench? Go to him, for he too has come for your sake. Leave the vanities of the past and long for the beauties of the present. Those are abominable; these are desirable and eternal. Copy your former ways: anoint with perfume the one who made the perfume; coax the one who wishes to save you. You have found a lover greater than all the lovers you have had. By loving them you poured many sins into yourself; if you love him, he himself will forgive you even the former sins that you gained from them.” With these thoughts she slips into the house and says: “I withdraw from my old evils; I find the new goods and agree to them. I renounce the evil one and join myself to the good. For I have heard David saying, ‘Come to him and be enlightened,’ and the Lord himself saying, ‘Draw near to me, and I will draw near to you.’ I too draw near to God, but I am afraid: I am the sinner coming to the sinless one, the mire coming to the ointment. Yet I hold as a pledge of his compassion the voice that says, ‘Come to me, all you sinners, and I will give you rest.’ So I will go. He does not reproach me. He does not say to me, ‘Get away from me, sinner! Until now you lived in darkness, and now you have come to see me, the sun of righteousness?’ But why do I deliberate? I take ointment and go to him. I make the Pharisee's house a place of enlightenment, and with the streams of my tears I prepare a font for myself. With the alabaster flask of ointment I receive the seal of the faithful upon my forehead. By repentance I am cleansed of my sins, and by his healing word I escape the snares of the devil. Nothing is hopeless for me. I know that in the Old Testament Rahab the harlot had a dwelling of sin by the gate of the city. Yet she received the spies of Israel, and as the reward for her hospitality she gained life. For Jesus the son of Nun, who saved her, was a type of the true Jesus; Jesus the son of Nun gave the harlot a good reward for the spies. If, then, the name of Jesus provided salvation and forgiveness of sins in those days, will the true Jesus now, the virgin born of a virgin, thrust away a harlot who receives him as a guest and anoints his feet with ointment? Will he not grant her remission of sins? But there Rahab let the spies go, while I stay and hold fast the one I have longed for. He is not, as with her, a spy sent to look over a city, but the Overseer of all human souls. Behold, as I said before, the time I longed to see has come. The day has dawned for me, and the sun of righteousness, and the acceptable year of the Lord, and a great visitation from God. For truly the dayspring from on high has visited us, to shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death. The Master is lodging in the house of Simon; let me go to him. And what shall I do? Shall I weep, as Hannah wept over her barrenness? But Simon will think I am drunk, just as Eli the high priest once thought of Hannah. Then shall I stay at Christ's feet, praying in my heart and weeping? This is what I will do.”

The harlot's faith worked together with her pure intention. She went to the man who sold ointment and began to say to him: “A great friend has come to me, greater than all the sons of men. So if you have ointment worthy of him, give it to me, so that I may make a worthy offering to the one I love so worthily, who has set my heart and my inmost being on fire. Do not worry about the price. If I must, I am ready to sell even my body and bones to pay for it, so that I may have at least some small thing to offer to the one who so wishes to cleanse me.” He saw the warmth and resolve of her faith and said to her: “Tell me, who is this one you long for, that he has warmed your love so much? What do you expect to receive from him in return for this ointment?” She said to him: “What are you saying to me, man? You are ignorant; you do not know what you are saying. He is able to give me something worth this ointment, even though no one can give him anything that matches his dignity. Neither heaven itself, nor earth, nor anyone in this world can be compared with the one who has come to me. You regard me as worthless, but he in his love for mankind has counted me worthy and freed me from my sins. He is the Son of David according to the flesh; that is why he is beautiful to look upon, for David said of him, ‘Fairer in beauty than the sons of men.’ He is the Son of God. I have not seen him, but when I heard about him I was wounded with longing. Michal the daughter of Saul loved David, left the palace and followed him in his poverty. And I am selling my own wealth, though I gathered it wickedly, to buy ointment, and I am running to him who came from David and became poor for my sake.” The faithful harlot took the ointment and ran to the house of the Pharisee as though she had been invited. The Pharisee saw the harlot holding Jesus' feet and anointing them, and the whole house filled with the fragrance of the ointment. He reasoned within himself and said: “If this man were a prophet, he would have perceived who the woman touching him is, and that she is a sinner.” He found fault with the harlot's boldness, since she had shamelessly come near and touched him. He also blamed the Master himself for thoughtlessly receiving everyone who came to him. Condemning him for ignorance, he said within himself: “What a state of affairs! I invited him to dinner as one of the prophets. Everyone who lives in the city knows this woman, and everyone recognizes her, yet this man did not know her. If he were a prophet, he would have known who the woman is.” But Christ, who tests hearts and minds, saw the Pharisee's thoughts. While Simon's reflections were tossed about, Christ became a calm within him and said to him: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” He said, “Teacher, say it.” He said to him: “I seemed blameworthy to you because I did not put the harlot to shame but covered her. It seemed blameworthy to you that I did not turn away from the sinner but welcomed her. It seemed blameworthy to you that I did not drive her off but justified her. It seemed blameworthy to you that I was not angry but was softened. It seemed blameworthy to you that I called back the woman who wished to flee from her own iniquities. You ought to rejoice over one who fell and rose again, yet you are grieved at what is good. But your blame is unreasonable. Judge this matter that I am about to tell you. A certain creditor had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When neither could pay, the creditor forgave both of them their bonds. Which of them, then, ought to love him more?” He said, “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.” Then, turning toward the woman, he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman, whom you have rejected? You did not deign to wash my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears. You did not give me a kiss of love, but she has not stopped kissing my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. But learn, Pharisee, who the creditor is and who the debtors are. I am the creditor of the two, of you and of her; and not only of you two, but of all people. I have given all people what they have received from me: soul, breath, body, senses, knowledge, movement. The creditor does not demand that you repay in full what you received. If you cannot repay, then beg him to forgive you the loan. But if you can neither repay nor think it right to beg for forgiveness, at least do not be shameless, talking much and resisting. Be silent like this harlot. She saw her many debts and said within herself, ‘What shall I say, or what shall I answer? If I want to say, “I do not owe the debt,” he knows all things; he himself knows how much I owe and how long I have been liable.’ So, seeing that he knows all things and that none of the evils she had done escapes him, she came in silence, weeping, and by confessing all her debts in her heart she won God's favor. So you too be silent, Pharisee, so that the Lord may forgive you your debt. You are condemned yourself, so do not condemn the condemned woman. You are worthless yourself, so do not despise the woman who is despised. Be still. I have no need of what is yours or of what is hers; I have come to forgive the debt of you both. For I am the merciful creditor of the two of you. And I am merciful not only to you, but to all who have nothing to repay, if only they confess the debt and through repentance ask me to forgive them the bond. If anyone, then, is in debt and comes to the grace of baptism, through it he is freed from the debt. Go, then. Behold, you have been released from your debts, and by grace you have been freed from all liability. Once the first bond has been torn up, do not bring another bond upon yourselves again.” But, O Lord and Master Jesus Christ, I have neither the means nor the strength to repay you what I owe. (For through my many iniquities I have wickedly squandered both the principal and the interest.) Do not demand of me what you supplied me, the principal of the soul and the interest of the flesh. Instead, as the lover of mankind, lighten for me the burden of my debts, and say to me too, as you said to the harlot: “Your many sins are forgiven.” For you alone are sinless and good and loving toward mankind, and you forgive sins. To you belongs all glory, honor and worship, together with your Father who is without beginning, and your all-holy, good and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
